title: UK critical mineral supply chains exposed, warn MPs
gist: A House of Commons committee report finds the UK cannot show it passes any of ten tests for secure critical mineral supply, identifying refining (the midstream) as the chokepoint and recycling as the opportunity. Benchmark data show China's refining dominance (87% of rare earths, 97% of processed dysprosium, 66% of lithium chemicals), UK lithium refining covering under a fifth of 2030 demand, zero UK black mass refining, and a proposed Critical Minerals Finance Facility modeled on US tools like the MP Materials stake and $110,000/t PrNd floor.

insights.claim: The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee reported on 5 November that the UK government cannot demonstrate it passes any of the ten tests the MPs say are needed for secure critical mineral supply chains.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
entities: House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee
insights.so_what: Formal parliamentary pressure raises odds of UK policy support and funding for domestic critical minerals projects.
insights.locator: MPs warn the UK government cannot

insights.claim: Across strategic mineral supply chains, refining rather than mining is often the crucial bottleneck to supply security.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Midstream processing assets, not mines, are where scarcity value and policy support concentrate.
insights.quote: Across strategic supply chains, refining is often the crucial bottleneck to supply security rather than mining.

insights.claim: Benchmark's Caspar Rawles told MPs that the critical gap in the UK supply chain is the midstream, namely chemical processing and anode and cathode production.
insights.speaker: Caspar Rawles
insights.so_what: UK policy funding is likely to target chemical refining and cathode/anode plants, the segments with least domestic capacity.
insights.quote: The critical gap at the moment in the UK supply chain particularly is the midstream
insights.locator: The critical gap at the moment

insights.claim: China accounts for around two-thirds of rare earths mining in 2026 but is forecast to produce 87% of global refined rare earths output, according to Benchmark's Rare Earths Service.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: China's leverage sits disproportionately in processing, so ex-China refiners are the scarcest strategic asset.

insights.claim: For heavy rare earths, China accounts for 38% of mined dysprosium but 97% of processed dysprosium.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Heavy rare earth separation is the most acute single-country dependency, a key target for Western capital and export-control risk.
insights.quote: China accounts for 38% of mined dysprosium but 97% of the processed material

insights.claim: China produces 66% of the world's lithium chemicals despite accounting for only 25% of primary lithium output.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Lithium miners outside China remain dependent on Chinese converters, supporting the case for ex-China lithium refineries.

themes.theme: UK lithium and rare earth capacity gap

insights.claim: UK refined lithium output is forecast to rise from 3,900 tonnes LCE in 2026 to around 20,000 tonnes by 2030, less than a fifth of the 112,800 tonnes LCE of UK lithium demand expected by 2030, per Benchmark's written evidence.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: The UK will remain structurally import-dependent for lithium chemicals through 2030, a durable demand sink for allied suppliers.

insights.claim: The UK has no primary rare earths mining or refining; its only commercial rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing facility, HyProMag, opened in January 2026 with an eventual capacity of 300 tonnes of NdFeB magnets per year.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Magnet recycling is the UK's only foothold in rare earths, positioning HyProMag as a strategic national asset.
insights.locator: The UK has no primary rare earths

insights.claim: High energy costs are a major concern for UK refineries, with one UK nickel refiner telling the committee that electricity at its UK site costs nearly 60% more than in France.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Power-price disadvantage undermines UK midstream competitiveness unless offset by subsidies or energy support.
insights.quote: electricity at its UK site costs nearly 60% more than in France
insights.locator: Energy costs are a major concern

insights.claim: Caspar Rawles told MPs the UK will not be self-sufficient in critical minerals because it is a small, densely populated island where land and energy are expensive.
insights.speaker: Caspar Rawles
insights.so_what: Realistic UK strategy is allied sourcing, recycling and targeted midstream bets rather than full domestic supply chains.
insights.quote: Obviously the UK is not going to be self-sufficient in these minerals
insights.locator: Obviously the UK is not going

insights.claim: Committee chair Liam Byrne argued Britain cannot re-arm, build AI or deliver net zero without securing the minerals those technologies depend on.
insights.speaker: Liam Byrne
insights.so_what: Framing minerals as defence, AI and climate infrastructure broadens the political coalition for funding.
insights.quote: We cannot re-arm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

themes.theme: Recycling and black mass refining gap

insights.claim: Caspar Rawles argued that as a relatively wealthy nation, the UK holds substantial minerals embedded in products such as EVs, energy storage and household batteries, making recycling an opportunity.
insights.speaker: Caspar Rawles
insights.so_what: Urban mining is positioned as the UK's comparative advantage in critical minerals.

insights.claim: The UK has around 22ktpa of battery pre-treatment (shredding to black mass) capacity installed but no black mass refining capacity, so the value in UK black mass is captured by overseas refiners.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Black mass hydrometallurgical refining is the missing UK link and a likely target for policy support and investment.
insights.quote: the UK has no black mass refining capacity, meaning the value contained within the material is lost to refiners overseas

insights.claim: There is 58ktpa of UK black mass refining capacity in the 2030 pipeline, but Benchmark says there is no guarantee it will come online without a supportive business environment.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Pipeline capacity is contingent on policy; investors should discount announced UK recycling projects absent government support.
insights.quote: there is no guarantee this capacity will come online unless there is a supportive business environment

insights.claim: The committee report recommends a UK Critical Minerals Finance Facility bringing together public financial institutions to deploy grants, equity, debt, guarantees and offtake agreements for strategic projects at home and abroad.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A state-backed financing vehicle would de-risk UK and allied critical-mineral projects and could anchor offtakes.
insights.quote: capable of bringing together the UK’s public financial institutions and deploying grants, equity, debt, guarantees and offtake agreements needed to accelerate strategically important projects at home and abroad
insights.locator: The need for new critical minerals finance

insights.claim: The proposed UK facility could take equity stakes, sign long-term offtakes and set price floors, mirroring US tools such as the government stake in MP Materials and a PrNd price floor of $110,000/t.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Price floors and state equity are becoming the Western template, supporting floor-protected economics for ex-China rare earth producers.

insights.claim: Caspar Rawles said billions are needed for a functioning UK supply chain, and the government must decide how much to support the industry at all costs for national security versus how much to invest for economic prosperity.
insights.speaker: Caspar Rawles
insights.so_what: The national-security vs. prosperity split determines whether UK support will be uneconomic-at-any-cost or return-driven, shaping which projects get funded.
insights.quote: Billions need to be poured into this to make it function and give us a fully functioning supply chain
